subject: English
description: Single-word substitutions for phrases; high-hit SSC PYQ vocab

questions.stem: ONE-WORD substitution for 'a person who knows many languages':

options.option_text: Bilingual (only two languages)
Polyglot (many languages)
Linguist (any language scholar)
Monolingual (just one language)

questions.explanation: POLYGLOT (Greek 'poly' = many + 'glotta' = tongue) = person who knows / speaks MANY languages. BILINGUAL = 2; TRILINGUAL = 3; MONOLINGUAL = 1; MULTILINGUAL = 2+ (often 3+). LINGUIST = scholar who STUDIES languages (theory) — not necessarily knows many. SSC PYQ favourite.

questions.stem: ONE-WORD for 'fear of confined / closed spaces':

options.option_text: Hydrophobia (fear of water)
Claustrophobia (closed-spaces fear)
Acrophobia (fear of heights)
Agoraphobia (open-spaces fear)

questions.explanation: Common PHOBIA list: CLAUSTROPHOBIA (Latin claustrum = closed) = closed spaces; ACROPHOBIA (acro = high) = heights; AGORAPHOBIA (agora = open marketplace) = open spaces; HYDROPHOBIA = water (also rabies symptom); ARACHNOPHOBIA = spiders; OPHIDIOPHOBIA = snakes; XENOPHOBIA = strangers / foreigners; PYROPHOBIA = fire; NYCTOPHOBIA = darkness; HEMOPHOBIA = blood; THANATOPHOBIA = death; TRISKAIDEKAPHOBIA = number 13.

questions.stem: ONE-WORD for 'a government run by a religious authority':

options.option_text: Democracy (rule by the people)
Theocracy (rule by religious leaders)
Aristocracy (rule by the nobility)
Plutocracy (rule by wealthy elite)

questions.explanation: Forms of GOVERNMENT (-cracy = rule, -archy = ruler): DEMOCRACY (demos = people); THEOCRACY (theo = god; e.g., Vatican, Iran); MONARCHY (one ruler); OLIGARCHY (few ruling); ARISTOCRACY (best class — nobility); PLUTOCRACY (wealth); MERITOCRACY (merit); BUREAUCRACY (officials); TECHNOCRACY (technical experts); GERONTOCRACY (old people); KAKISTOCRACY (worst people!); KLEPTOCRACY (corrupt leaders enriching themselves); ANARCHY (no government). Common SSC PYQ.

questions.stem: ONE-WORD for 'a person who eats both plants and meat':

options.option_text: Carnivore, who eats only meat
Omnivore, who eats both
Herbivore, who eats only plants
Insectivore, who eats only insects

questions.explanation: Diet types (-vore = eater): OMNIVORE (omni = all); CARNIVORE (carni = meat); HERBIVORE (herba = plants); FRUGIVORE (frutus = fruit); PISCIVORE (piscis = fish); INSECTIVORE (insectus); GRANIVORE (grain); NECTARIVORE (nectar); CARRION/SCAVENGER eater; HAEMATOPHAGE (blood). Humans are biologically OMNIVORES. Vegetarians/vegans are humans choosing not to eat meat.
questions.subject: English

options.option_text: Misanthrope (hates humanity)
Misogamist (hates marriage)
Misogynist (hates women)
Bigamist (married to two)

questions.explanation: Mis- prefix = hate. MISOGAMIST (gamos = marriage) = hates marriage; MISOGYNIST (gyne = woman) = hates women; MISANDRIST (andros = man) = hates men; MISANTHROPE (anthropos = man/human) = hates humanity / mankind in general. Marriage states: BIGAMY = 2 spouses; POLYGAMY = many spouses; MONOGAMY = 1; CELIBACY = unmarried, esp. for religious vows.

questions.stem: ONE-WORD for 'speech that is so eloquent + persuasive that it carries the audience':

options.option_text: Tirade, an angry attacking speech
Oration, a persuasive formal speech
Soliloquy, a one-actor stage talk
Diatribe, a bitter critical speech

questions.explanation: Types of speeches: ORATION (= formal, eloquent public speech, e.g., Lincoln's Gettysburg Address); ELOQUENCE (= eloquent speech style); SOLILOQUY (= speaking alone on stage; thought aloud, e.g., Hamlet's 'To be or not to be'); MONOLOGUE (= long uninterrupted speech by one person); DIATRIBE / TIRADE = harsh, abusive criticism; HARANGUE = lengthy, aggressive lecture; PANEGYRIC = praise speech; EULOGY = praise of the dead. SSC + UPSC frequent.

questions.stem: ONE-WORD for 'a place where birds are kept':

options.option_text: Aquarium (place for fish)
Aviary (place for birds)
Apiary (place for bees)
Hatchery (eggs are hatched)

questions.explanation: Animal-keeping places: AVIARY (avis = bird); AQUARIUM (aqua = water → fish); APIARY (apis = bee); KENNEL (dogs); STABLE / BARN (horses, cattle); HUTCH (rabbits); PEN (sheep, pigs); WAREN / WARREN (rabbits in wild); HATCHERY (eggs hatching, esp. fish, poultry); ZOO / VIVARIUM = many animals. Plant places: GREENHOUSE / CONSERVATORY / NURSERY / ARBORETUM (trees); ORCHARD (fruit trees); VINEYARD (grapes).

questions.stem: Which one-word substitution correctly describes a person who walks about during sleep?

options.option_text: Insomniac — one who suffers from chronic sleeplessness
Somnambulist — one who walks during the sleep state
Narcoleptic — one prone to sudden irresistible sleep attacks
Somniloquist — one who talks aloud during sleep

questions.explanation: Somnambulist is the precise term for walking during sleep (Latin: somnus = sleep, ambulare = to walk). Somniloquist is the most tempting distractor as it shares the 'somn-' root, but it refers to talking in sleep, not walking — a distinction examiners frequently exploit.

questions.stem: Which one-word substitution best describes an inscription engraved on a tomb or a memorial stone?

options.option_text: Elegy — a mournful poem lamenting the death of someone
Eulogy — a speech of high praise delivered at a funeral
Epitaph — an inscription written on or for a tombstone
Obituary — a printed notice of death published in newspapers

questions.explanation: Epitaph derives from Greek 'epi' (upon) + 'taphos' (tomb) and specifically means an inscription carved on a gravestone. Eulogy is the chief distractor — it also honours the dead — but a eulogy is a spoken tribute at a funeral, not something inscribed on stone.

questions.stem: Which one-word substitution applies to a person who collects and studies coins, medals, and currency?

options.option_text: Philatelist — one who collects and studies postage stamps
Antiquarian — one who studies and deals in antique objects
Numismatist — one who collects and studies coins and currency
Bibliophile — one who is a passionate collector of rare books

questions.explanation: Numismatist is the exact term for a collector/scholar of coins, medals, and currency (Latin: numisma = coin). Philatelist is the classic wrong answer — it refers to stamp collectors, not coin collectors. Both are 'collector' words, which is how examiners engineer the confusion.

questions.stem: Which one-word substitution best describes a person who fraudulently claims to possess expert skill or special knowledge they do not actually have?

options.option_text: Pedant — one who displays learning in a tedious and irritating manner
Hypocrite — one who claims virtues or beliefs they do not actually hold
Dilettante — one who engages in arts or study without deep commitment
Charlatan — one who falsely claims professional skill or special expertise

questions.explanation: Charlatan (from Italian 'ciarlare' = to chatter) denotes fraudulent claims of professional or medical expertise. Hypocrite is the strongest distractor but relates to moral pretence — claiming to be virtuous while acting otherwise — not to fakery about skills or knowledge.

questions.stem: Which one-word substitution specifically refers to the social practice of one man being married to more than one woman at the same time?

options.option_text: Polygamy — practice of having multiple spouses of either sex simultaneously
Polyandry — practice of one woman having multiple husbands at once
Bigamy — the illegal act of marrying while still legally wedded to another
Polygyny — practice of one man having multiple wives simultaneously

questions.explanation: Polygyny is the specific term for multiple wives (Greek: polys = many, gyne = woman). Polygamy is the most frequent wrong answer in exams — it is a broader umbrella term for any multiple-spouse arrangement regardless of gender, and does not exclusively mean multiple wives.

questions.stem: Which one-word substitution correctly refers to a person who has recently been converted to a new religion or newly initiated into a belief system or organisation?

options.option_text: Apostate — one who has formally abandoned their previously held religious faith
Proselyte — one who actively persuades others to adopt their own religion or cause
Zealot — one who shows extreme and uncompromising devotion to a cause or religion
Neophyte — one recently converted to a doctrine or newly initiated into a group

questions.explanation: Neophyte (Greek: neos = new, phytos = planted) means a recent convert or newly initiated member of any group or belief system. Proselyte is the top distractor — it can also mean a convert, but standard usage favours it to mean one who has been converted from another faith (especially to Judaism), and it is often confused with one who proselytises (urges others to convert), making the meaning ambiguous.

questions.stem: Which one-word substitution describes the practice of maintaining multiple simultaneous romantic relationships with the full knowledge and informed consent of all partners involved?

options.option_text: Polygamy — legally or socially sanctioned marriage to multiple spouses at once
Polyamory — consensual engagement in multiple simultaneous loving relationships
Libertinism — the unrestrained pursuit of pleasure without moral or social limits
Promiscuity — indiscriminate sexual activity with many casual and transient partners

questions.explanation: Polyamory (Greek: polys = many + Latin: amor = love) precisely denotes consensual, ethical multi-partner romantic involvement with transparency among all parties. Polygamy is the strongest distractor but refers specifically to multiple formal spousal unions (legal/ceremonial), does not require mutual consent of all parties, and excludes non-marital relationships — distinctions that define the harder tier of one-word substitution questions.
